title: Onboarding That Actually Helps New Teammates
summary: Good onboarding gives new teammates a map, a buddy, small real tasks and a safe place to ask. What to prepare, what research says, and how to tell if it's working.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Monday, 9:40am. Your new teammate has a laptop that's still installing things, a "Welcome aboard!" message in chat and six browser tabs asking for access requests. Everyone's friendly, and everyone's busy. When you ask how it's going, they say "All good!" Meanwhile they're collecting a list of questions they don't yet know how to ask, or who to ask.

That first week is the new person's first real look at how your team handles questions, mistakes and things nobody wrote down. You can say you value ownership in every all-hands. If week one is mostly silent guessing, that's the lesson they'll actually take home.

This post is about onboarding from the team's side: what to prepare, who does what, and how to tell if it's working. If you're the new person, the companion piece is on asking for help early.

Aim for orientation before output

Pushing someone to "ship something on day one" usually produces a bit of theater: a one-line PR picked because it's safe, a rushed architecture tour nobody remembers, a calendar so full of intro calls there's no time to think. A better goal for the first weeks is orientation. By the end, the new person should know what the product does, who uses it, how the team makes decisions, which parts of the code are risky and where to go when they're stuck.

Tasks still matter a lot, just for a different reason. A team at Microsoft interviewed 32 developers who had moved into a new team and 15 managers who onboarded them, then checked the findings with surveys of 189 developers and 37 managers. They found that most of onboarding is the tasks themselves, and that's where new developers learn the system, build confidence, meet the team and earn its recognition (Ju et al., A Case Study of Onboarding in Software Teams, ICSE 2021). So the first tasks deserve real thought.

Tell the story before you hand out tickets

Someone can install every dependency and still have no idea why the system exists. Before the first ticket, give them the plain story:

  • What customers are trying to get done, and which two or three flows matter most.
  • Which incidents shaped today's rules. "We added that approval step after the double-charge bug in March" explains more than any diagram.
  • Why the codebase looks the way it does, including the messy parts. A weird folder is much less scary once someone explains how it got that way.

Without that story, every folder feels like a test of whether you're smart enough to be here.

Give the first month a rhythm

The Microsoft study named three ways managers pick early tasks. "Simple-Complex" starts with quick, well-defined tasks and makes them harder over time. "Priority-First" hands out whatever is top of the backlog. "Exploration-Based" gives open, under-defined problems. The authors note that "challenging tasks early in the onboarding process could spur fears and low confidence", unless the team backs the person up, for example by pairing them with an experienced developer. They think exploration works better for experienced hires, though they flag that as untested.

A rough rhythm that follows that advice:

  • Day one: access, local setup, a product walkthrough and a named buddy. That's plenty for a first day.
  • Week one: one or two small, real changes that touch the product, with a patient review.
  • Week two: a real feature area with a teammate nearby, past the cleanup tickets.
  • End of month one: a bounded task they own end to end, and enough context to ask sharper questions in planning.

Adjust for seniority. A staff engineer can handle an open question in week two. A new grad will get more from three quick wins first.

Give them a buddy, and make the buddy a real role

A buddy isn't a manager and isn't an on-call rescue service. They're the safe first door: the person you can ask "sorry, what's the BFF again?" without feeling silly. A good buddy does more than answer. They hand over the map: which channel is for what, which docs are still true, who owns which service, and when to ask in public so everyone learns.

It pays to take the role seriously. When Microsoft piloted a buddy program with 600 employees, 56% of new hires who met their buddy at least once in the first 90 days said the buddy helped them get productive quickly. That rose to 73% for two to three meetings, 86% for four to eight, and 97% for more than eight (Microsoft, Every new employee needs an onboarding buddy). Those numbers are self-reported, and they only show that more meetings went with better ratings. Still, the direction is hard to miss: the more often people met, the more useful they said the buddy was. Put a recurring 20-minute slot on both calendars for the first month, and give the buddy real time for it in sprint planning.

Write docs for someone in their first week

Most docs are written by people who already know the system, so they skip exactly the parts a new person needs. A few checks help:

  • The setup guide lists exact versions, the three errors everyone hits and what "it works" looks like on screen.
  • Architecture notes explain trade-offs and old decisions, beyond drawing boxes.
  • Runbooks say how to tell whether a service is healthy.

Good docs won't replace conversation. They make it sharper, because the new person can say "step 4 fails with this error" instead of "setup doesn't work."

The first PR teaches the culture

The first pull request should be real enough to touch the product and small enough to finish without understanding the whole company. The review matters more than the code. This is where the team shows its actual standards: how much context goes in a PR description, what tests look like here, how comments are worded and what disagreement feels like. People learn more about your culture from their first review than from the onboarding slides. How to Review Code Kindly covers the reviewer's side in detail.

It also helps to pick early tasks that need a conversation with someone outside the buddy. In the Microsoft study, tasks that required collaboration "force new developers to establish new social connections." Just go easy on tasks that wait on another team, since the same paper found that waiting on feedback can drain motivation.

Ask three questions every week

Plenty of people won't say "I'm lost" in a group channel, especially while they're still proving they belong. The Microsoft paper recommends frequent 1:1s in the first few weeks and a psychologically safe environment. A short private check-in covers a lot of that. Ask the same three questions each week:

  1. What surprised you?
  2. What's still confusing?
  3. What should we explain better for the next person?

The answers help the new person, and they also show you the rough edges everyone else got used to. If every new hire fights the local setup, the fix is a better setup script, however impressive their persistence. If everyone asks the same architecture question, write the answer down once. A new teammate is the only person on the team who can still see those problems clearly, so use that while it lasts.

Try this week

  • Write the one-page "story of our product" for your team: who uses it, the flows that matter, two incidents that shaped the rules.
  • Pick a buddy for the next hire now, and block a recurring 20-minute slot for their first month.
  • Ask the last person who joined which setup step broke for them, then fix that step.
  • Tag three small, real tickets as "good first task" so they're ready on day one.
  • Add the three check-in questions to your 1:1 notes template.

Think back to your own best first week. The details you remember are probably small: someone who explained an acronym without making it awkward, a README that actually worked, a review comment that taught you something without embarrassing you. That's your onboarding system, and you can improve it a little with every person who joins.

faqs.q: What should a new engineer do in their first week?
faqs.a: Get access and a working local setup, walk through the product, meet a named buddy and finish one or two small, real changes with a patient review. The goal for the first weeks is orientation: knowing what the product does, who uses it, how decisions get made and where to go when stuck.

faqs.q: What kind of first tasks work best for new developers?
faqs.a: A Microsoft study of onboarding (Ju et al., ICSE 2021) found that most of onboarding is the tasks themselves, and that's where new developers learn the system, build confidence and connect with the team. Starting with quick, well-defined tasks and raising difficulty over time is safer for less experienced people, since challenging tasks too early can hurt confidence unless someone pairs with them.

faqs.q: Does an onboarding buddy really help?
faqs.a: In Microsoft's buddy pilot with 600 employees, 56% of new hires who met their buddy at least once in 90 days said the buddy helped them get productive quickly, rising to 97% for those who met more than eight times. The numbers are self-reported, but they suggest regular meetings matter more than a single intro.

Exact tool versions, the common setup errors and what a working setup looks like. Architecture notes that explain trade-offs and old decisions. Runbooks that say how to tell whether a service is healthy. Write all of it for someone in their first week.

faqs.q: How do I know if onboarding is working?
faqs.a: Ask the new person three questions every week in a private check-in: what surprised you, what's still confusing and what should we explain better for the next person. Then fix the recurring answers, like a broken setup step or a missing architecture note.
